questions.title: Unit vs Integration vs End-to-End Testing
questions.direct_answer: Unit tests verify individual methods/classes in isolation using mocks, run in milliseconds. Integration tests verify components working together (e.g., controller + service + real DB), run in seconds. E2E tests verify full user journeys through the deployed application, run in minutes. The testing pyramid recommends many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few E2E tests.

sections.title: The Testing Pyramid Isn't About Ratios — It's About Feedback Speed vs Confidence
sections.content:
The testing pyramid puts unit tests at the base, integration tests in the middle, and end-to-end tests at the top. Most explanations focus on quantity ("more unit tests, fewer E2E tests"), but the real insight is about **feedback loops and failure diagnosis.**

A unit test runs in milliseconds, tests one class in isolation, and when it fails, tells you exactly what broke. An integration test runs in seconds, verifies that components work together (Spring context, database, HTTP), and when it fails, might point to the component or the interaction. An end-to-end test runs in minutes, verifies the full user flow, and when it fails, tells you *something* is broken — but finding what requires investigation.

The pyramid's shape reflects this trade-off: you want **fast, precise tests as the foundation** and **slow, broad tests as verification.** The anti-pattern is the ice cream cone — mostly E2E tests with few unit tests. This means every failure triggers a 15-minute investigation instead of a 15-second method name. Tests become so slow that developers stop running them locally, and CI becomes the only feedback loop.

Unit tests give you speed. Integration tests give you confidence that components connect correctly. E2E tests give you confidence that the system works as a user would experience it.

sections.title: Unit vs Integration vs E2E — What Each Level Proves
sections.content:
| Aspect | Unit Test | Integration Test | E2E Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | One class/method | Multiple components + infrastructure | Full system through UI/API |
| Dependencies | Mocked | Real (DB, Spring context, HTTP) | Everything real |
| Speed | Milliseconds | Seconds | Minutes |
| Failure diagnosis | Exact method | Component or interaction | "Something is broken" |
| Frameworks | JUnit 5 + Mockito | `@SpringBootTest`, `@DataJpaTest` | Selenium, Playwright, REST Assured |
| When to write | Every business rule | Database queries, API contracts, configs | Critical user journeys only |
| Maintenance cost | Low | Medium | High (brittle, environment-dependent) |

The table reveals the cost curve: E2E tests are the most expensive to write, the slowest to run, and the hardest to diagnose. Investing heavily in E2E over unit tests maximizes cost while minimizing feedback speed.

sections.title: What to Test at Each Level — The Decision Framework
sections.content:
**Unit test when:** the logic is in your code — business rules, calculations, transformations, validation. If the method takes inputs and produces outputs without external dependencies, it's a unit test. This includes services with mocked repositories, mappers, validators, and utility classes.

**Integration test when:** correctness depends on how components interact — JPA queries returning correct results, REST endpoints accepting the right request format, Spring Security denying unauthorized requests, configuration loading correctly. The test verifies the *wiring*, not the logic.

**E2E test when:** you need confidence that the full system works for critical user journeys — login, checkout, payment, onboarding. Keep these to 5-15 scenarios that cover the most important flows. Every additional E2E test adds maintenance cost and CI time.

The practical rule: **if you can test it with a unit test, don't write an integration test.** If the integration test covers it, don't add an E2E test. Push testing to the lowest level that still gives you confidence.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The testing pyramid puts unit tests at the base, integration tests in the middle, and end-to-end tests at the top. The real reason for that shape isn't quantity — it's feedback speed versus confidence. Each level proves something different, and misusing the pyramid is the most common cause of slow, brittle CI pipelines.

**Unit tests — fastest feedback, narrowest proof**
- A unit test runs one class in isolation with mocked collaborators — milliseconds per test, immediate feedback on business logic, no infrastructure required
- They prove your logic is correct given assumptions about dependencies; they do not prove the system works end-to-end — that's by design
- If you have to mock extensively to test a class, that's not a test problem — it's a design signal that the class has too many responsibilities

**Integration tests — prove the wiring**
- An integration test exercises multiple layers together with real infrastructure — your `OrderService` calling a real PostgreSQL database through JPA, not an H2 stub
- Testcontainers is the modern standard: real Postgres in Docker during the test run, identical to production SQL dialect, catches dialect-specific query bugs that H2 misses
- These run in seconds, not milliseconds — keep them focused on proving the integration points, not re-proving business rules already covered by unit tests

**End-to-end tests — prove the user journey**
- E2E tests drive the full system — HTTP through the API, through the service layer, through the database, and assert the response; they prove everything works assembled
- They are expensive: slow to run, fragile to infrastructure changes, hard to debug failures — reserve them for the critical happy paths that represent real user value
- A test suite that's mostly E2E tests is called an ice cream cone — it's inverted and expensive to maintain

The pyramid shape isn't a rule — it's an economic argument: push testing to the lowest level that gives confidence in what you're testing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Unit tests = milliseconds, single class, mocked deps** — they prove logic correctness given assumptions; they do not prove the system works end-to-end
- **Integration tests = real infrastructure** — Testcontainers over H2; real PostgreSQL catches dialect-specific bugs that H2's SQL mode masks
- **E2E tests = full user journey** — HTTP through the system; most expensive, most fragile, fewest in number; reserve for critical happy paths
- **Ice cream cone = inverted pyramid** — mostly E2E tests is the anti-pattern; slow CI, fragile suite, hard to diagnose failures
- **Feedback speed determines the level** — if the concept can be proven by a unit test, don't write an integration test for it; if it requires real DB queries, don't mock

questions.question: What is @SpringBootTest and when would you use its slice variants like @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest instead?
questions.title: @SpringBootTest and Its Slice Variants
questions.direct_answer: @SpringBootTest loads the full application context and is great for true integration tests, but is slow. Slice annotations load only the relevant portion: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, security), @DataJpaTest loads only the persistence layer (repositories, entities, DataSource). Use slices to get faster, more focused tests without bootstrapping the entire context.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every test — it is slow and causes context reloading; slices are much faster and more focused
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @WebMvcTest does NOT load the service layer, so you must mock services with @MockBean, and why that separation is intentional

sections.title: @SpringBootTest Loads Everything — That's Why It's Slow and Why Slices Exist
sections.content:
`@SpringBootTest` starts the full Spring application context — every bean, every auto-configuration, every component scan. This gives maximum fidelity but at a cost: context startup takes 5-30 seconds depending on the application. For a project with 200 tests all using `@SpringBootTest`, the test suite runs for 30+ minutes.

**Test slices** load only the parts of the context relevant to what you're testing. `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` loads the web layer — controller, filters, converters — but not services, repositories, or database connections. `@DataJpaTest` loads JPA repositories and an embedded H2 database but not controllers or services.

The performance difference is dramatic. A `@WebMvcTest` starts in under 2 seconds. The same test with `@SpringBootTest` takes 10-15 seconds because it loads the entire application including database connections, message brokers, and scheduled tasks that the test doesn't need.

Spring caches application contexts across tests with the same configuration — but slices with different `@MockBean` annotations create different cache keys, triggering new context creation. Minimizing distinct `@MockBean` combinations across test classes keeps context caching effective.

sections.title: Test Slice Selection — What Each Annotation Loads
sections.content:
| Annotation | What it loads | What it excludes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@SpringBootTest` | Everything | Nothing | Full integration tests, app startup verification |
| `@WebMvcTest` | Controllers, filters, `@ControllerAdvice` | Services, repositories, DB | Controller request/response testing |
| `@DataJpaTest` | JPA repos, `EntityManager`, H2/Testcontainers | Controllers, services | Repository query verification |
| `@WebFluxTest` | WebFlux controllers | Everything else | Reactive controller testing |
| `@JsonTest` | Jackson `ObjectMapper` | Everything else | JSON serialization/deserialization |
| `@RestClientTest` | `RestTemplate` / `WebClient` with mock server | Everything else | External API client testing |

The pattern: **use the narrowest slice that covers what you're testing.** If you're testing a controller's request mapping and validation, `@WebMvcTest` is faster and more focused than `@SpringBootTest`. If you're testing a JPA query, `@DataJpaTest` loads only what the repository needs.

sections.title: When @SpringBootTest Is Actually the Right Choice
Test Profile and Property Overrides — Isolating Test Configuration
sections.content:
Test slices often need different configuration than production. `@TestPropertySource(properties = "spring.jpa.show-sql=true")` overrides individual properties. `@ActiveProfiles("test")` activates a test-specific `application-test.yml` with test database URLs, disabled scheduling, and mock external service endpoints.

The hierarchy matters: `@TestPropertySource` overrides profile properties, which override `application.yml`. This lets you keep most configuration in the default file and override only what's test-specific.

One pattern that prevents test configuration drift: create a `src/test/resources/application-test.yml` that disables everything tests don't need — scheduled tasks (`spring.task.scheduling.enabled=false`), actuator endpoints, and Kafka auto-configuration. Tests start faster because Spring skips auto-configuration for components that aren't part of the test.

For `@DataJpaTest`, properties like `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop` ensure a clean schema per test run. Combined with `@Transactional` rollback, this gives complete test isolation without manual cleanup scripts.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@SpringBootTest` starts the full Spring application context — every bean, every auto-configuration, every component scan. This gives maximum fidelity at maximum cost: 5–30 seconds of context startup before a single assertion runs. For a project with 200 tests all using `@SpringBootTest`, that's minutes of overhead before the test logic begins.

**When to use each variant**
- `@SpringBootTest`: use for smoke tests and full integration tests that need everything assembled — verifying the application starts, testing cross-cutting configuration, end-to-end flows; not for individual component tests
- `@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)`: loads only the web layer — `DispatcherServlet`, filters, argument resolvers, `@ControllerAdvice` — but not `@Service` or `@Repository`; mock your services with `@MockBean`; runs in milliseconds
- `@DataJpaTest`: loads JPA, Spring Data repositories, and a database; by default substitutes H2; add `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` with Testcontainers to test against real PostgreSQL

**The `@MockBean` trap**
- Every `@MockBean` in a test class invalidates Spring's context cache for tests that don't share the exact same mock configuration — a new context loads for each different `@MockBean` combination
- The fix: centralize `@MockBean` declarations in a base test class that all tests in the suite extend; Spring reuses the same context for all subclasses
- Profile-aware configuration, active properties, and `@TestPropertySource` also affect cache keys — changes to these force context reloads

**Context caching**
- Spring caches the application context between test classes with identical configuration — if test class A and B both use `@DataJpaTest` with the same beans, the context starts once and is shared

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootTest` = full context, 5-30s startup** — maximum fidelity; use for smoke tests and full integration flows, not for individual component tests
- **`@WebMvcTest` = web layer only** — `DispatcherServlet` + filters + `@ControllerAdvice`; services must be `@MockBean`; millisecond startup; tests HTTP mapping and validation
- **`@DataJpaTest` = JPA + repositories** — add `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` with Testcontainers to test against real PostgreSQL instead of H2
- **`@MockBean` invalidates context cache** — each unique `@MockBean` combination forces a new context; centralize mock declarations in a base test class to keep suite fast
- **Context caching is the key to suite speed** — tests with identical configuration share one context; fragmented `@MockBean` usage is the #1 cause of slow Spring Boot test suites

questions.question: What is the difference between @Mock, @Spy, and @MockBean in Mockito/Spring Boot tests?
questions.title: Mockito: @Mock vs @Spy vs @MockBean
questions.direct_answer: @Mock creates a pure Mockito mock — all methods return default values unless stubbed; used in plain unit tests. @Spy wraps a real object, delegating to real methods unless overridden; useful when you want mostly real behaviour with one method stubbed. @MockBean creates a Mockito mock AND registers it in the Spring application context, replacing any existing bean of that type — required in @WebMvcTest and @SpringBootTest when you need to stub a Spring-managed dependency.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the distinction between plain Mockito and Spring-managed mocks, and when a spy is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @MockBean in plain unit tests (unnecessary and slow — it requires a Spring context to start) or using @Mock when you need Spring to inject the mock
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @MockBean causes the Spring context to be recreated if it wasn't already created with that mock, which can slow down suites — so centralise @MockBean usage in base test classes

sections.title: @Mock Is Fast and Free — @MockBean Loads Spring and Should Be Your Last Resort
sections.content:
Three annotations create test doubles in Java testing, and using the wrong one in the wrong context either slows your tests or makes them unreliable.

**`@Mock`** (Mockito) creates a mock object without Spring. It's fast — no context loading, no bean registration. Use it in plain unit tests where you control all dependencies through constructor injection. The mock returns defaults (null for objects, 0 for primitives, empty for collections) unless you configure behavior with `when().thenReturn()`.

**`@MockBean`** (Spring Boot Test) creates a mock AND registers it in the Spring application context, replacing the real bean. It requires a Spring context to exist — meaning it only works with `@SpringBootTest` or test slices. This is powerful but expensive: adding `@MockBean` in a test class may invalidate the cached context, forcing a full context reload.

**`@Spy`** (Mockito) wraps a real object — real method calls execute unless you override them with `when().thenReturn()`. This is useful when most of the object's behavior should be real but you need to override one specific method (e.g., a method that calls an external service).

The mistake: using `@MockBean` in plain unit tests. If you're testing a service with a mocked repository and no Spring context needed, `@Mock` with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` is 100x faster.

sections.title: @Mock vs @Spy vs @MockBean — The Decision Matrix
sections.content:
| Aspect | `@Mock` | `@Spy` | `@MockBean` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Framework | Mockito | Mockito | Spring Boot Test |
| Spring context required | No | No | Yes |
| Creates | Fake object, all methods stubbed | Wraps real object | Mock registered as Spring bean |
| Default behavior | Returns null/0/empty | Calls real methods | Returns null/0/empty |
| Speed | Instant | Instant | Requires context startup |
| Use when | Unit testing with DI | Need mostly real behavior | Integration test needs mock in context |
| Context cache impact | None | None | May invalidate cached context |

The table makes the cost clear: `@Mock` and `@Spy` are free. `@MockBean` potentially triggers a multi-second context reload.

sections.title: When Each One Is the Right Choice — With Code
ArgumentCaptor and verify() — Asserting What Was Called, Not Just What Was Returned
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Mockito's `@Mock`, `@Spy`, and Spring's `@MockBean` serve different purposes in different test contexts. Using the wrong one either slows your tests or makes them unreliable — `@MockBean` in a plain unit test is the most common mistake.

**`@Mock` — pure unit test isolation**
- `@Mock` creates a complete stub with no behavior — all methods return empty values (null, 0, empty list) unless you stub them with `when().thenReturn()`
- No Spring context is started — the mock exists purely in JVM memory; pair it with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` for automatic injection
- Use when testing a single class in isolation: `OrderService` with a mocked `OrderRepository` and `PaymentGateway` — the test runs in milliseconds, proves business logic only

**`@Spy` — partial mocking**
- A spy wraps a real object — the real method is called unless you explicitly stub it; useful when you want most real behavior but need to stub one method or verify calls
- Use `doReturn().when()` with spies, never `when().thenReturn()` — the latter calls the real method before the stub is applied, causing unexpected side effects
- Common use: spying on a `List` to verify `add()` was called a certain number of times, while letting the real list operations execute

**`@MockBean` — Spring integration tests**
- `@MockBean` registers a Mockito mock as a Spring bean in the test's ApplicationContext — needed when `@WebMvcTest` or `@DataJpaTest` loads a context and you need to mock a collaborator that would otherwise fail to wire
- Every unique `@MockBean` configuration creates a new Spring context — mixing `@MockBean` configurations across test classes fragments the context cache and slows the suite
- Never use `@MockBean` in plain unit tests — it requires Spring to start, which defeats the purpose of a fast unit test

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Mock` = JVM only, no Spring** — all methods return empty values by default; pair with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`; runs in milliseconds; use for unit tests
- **`@Spy` = real object wrapped** — calls real methods unless stubbed; always use `doReturn().when()` not `when().thenReturn()` with spies — the latter calls the real method before stubbing
- **`@MockBean` = Spring bean replacement** — registers a mock in the application context; needed for `@WebMvcTest`/`@DataJpaTest` tests; each unique combination forces a new context load
- **Never `@MockBean` in unit tests** — it starts a Spring context for no benefit; `@Mock` is the correct and faster alternative in plain JUnit tests
- **Context cache fragmentation** — consolidate `@MockBean` declarations into a base test class; `@WebMvcTest` tests that share the same mocks share the same context

questions.title: Testing with @DataJpaTest and Testcontainers
questions.direct_answer: Use @DataJpaTest with @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE) to prevent Spring from replacing your DataSource with H2. Declare a PostgreSQLContainer as a static @Container field and use @DynamicPropertySource to inject the container's JDBC URL, username, and password into the Spring context before it starts. This gives you tests that run against real Postgres with the same dialect, indexes, and constraints as production.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE) — without it Spring replaces your DataSource with H2 even when Testcontainers is configured

sections.title: H2 Lies About Your Queries — Testcontainers Runs the Real Database
sections.content:
`@DataJpaTest` auto-configures an embedded H2 database by default. This is fast but deceptive — H2's SQL dialect differs from MySQL and PostgreSQL in subtle ways. A query that works in H2 fails in production because H2 supports syntax that your production database doesn't, or handles NULLs differently, or has different collation rules.

Testcontainers launches a real database in a Docker container during the test. Your JPA queries run against the actual database engine you deploy to production — same SQL dialect, same type system, same edge cases. The setup takes a few seconds for container startup, but the queries execute against truth, not approximation.

The critical annotation: **`@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)`** tells Spring Boot NOT to replace your DataSource with an embedded database. Without it, `@DataJpaTest` ignores your `application-test.yml` DataSource configuration and uses H2 regardless of what you've configured.

The investment pays off when a production bug traces back to a query that worked in H2 but fails in PostgreSQL. Common examples: H2 accepts `GROUP BY 1` (positional reference) while some MySQL modes reject it. H2's `CONCAT` handles NULL differently than PostgreSQL. H2's `LIMIT/OFFSET` syntax works, but pagination edge cases with custom sorting behave differently. Testing against the real database catches these before production.

sections.title: The Testcontainers + @DataJpaTest Pattern
What to Actually Test in Repository Tests — Beyond findAll()
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@DataJpaTest` auto-configures a JPA environment for testing repositories and entity mappings. By default it replaces your DataSource with an embedded H2 database — which sounds convenient until a production query fails because H2 handles NULLs differently, doesn't support your PostgreSQL-specific window function, or accepts invalid SQL that PostgreSQL rejects.

**Why H2 is dangerous**
- H2's PostgreSQL compatibility mode is incomplete — `JSONB` columns, full-text search operators, `ILIKE`, and certain index types don't exist in H2; tests pass in H2, fail in production
- Schema migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) may use database-specific DDL that H2 can't parse — meaning your migration scripts are never tested against real SQL
- The fix is one annotation: `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` — this tells Spring to use your configured DataSource rather than replacing it with H2

**Testcontainers setup**

sections.title: MockMvc Tests the Controller Layer Without Starting a Server — That's Both Its Power and Its Limitation
sections.content:
MockMvc simulates HTTP requests through Spring's `DispatcherServlet` without starting a real HTTP server. No socket binding, no TCP overhead — requests go directly through the servlet pipeline. This makes controller tests fast (milliseconds) while still exercising the full Spring MVC stack: request mapping, parameter binding, validation, exception handling, and content negotiation.

The limitation: MockMvc bypasses the HTTP transport layer. Issues that only appear with a real server — CORS configuration, SSL, response compression, multipart parsing edge cases — won't be caught. For these, you need `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` with `TestRestTemplate`.

MockMvc pairs best with `@WebMvcTest`, which loads only the controller layer. Dependencies like services and repositories are mocked with `@MockBean`. This combination tests that your controller correctly maps requests, validates input, calls the right service method, and returns the right HTTP status and response body — without touching the database or any real service.

The key advantage of MockMvc over a real HTTP test: **speed and determinism.** No port binding, no network stack, no race conditions from async startup. A MockMvc test suite with 50 controller tests runs in under 5 seconds because the servlet simulation has zero network overhead. This makes it practical to test every request mapping, every validation rule, and every error response without slowing down the developer feedback loop.

How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MockMvc simulates HTTP requests through Spring's `DispatcherServlet` without starting a real HTTP server. No socket, no port binding — requests go directly through the servlet pipeline. This makes controller tests run in milliseconds while still exercising the full Spring MVC stack: request mapping, argument resolution, validation, and `@ControllerAdvice` exception handling.

**The two setup approaches**
- `@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)` is the correct approach for isolated controller tests — loads only the web layer, requires you to mock services with `@MockBean`, starts in milliseconds; this is the preferred approach
- `@SpringBootTest + @AutoConfigureMockMvc` loads the full context — useful when you need real service behavior in the test, but slow; avoid for pure controller testing

**What you can test with MockMvc**
- HTTP mapping: the right method is called for the right path and method — `perform(get("/orders/1"))` calls `getOrder(Long id)` not `getOrders()`
- Request validation: `@Valid` on the request body — `perform(post("/orders").content("{}"))` triggers `@NotNull` violations and you assert a 400 response with the right error shape
- Exception handling: your `@ControllerAdvice` maps a thrown `OrderNotFoundException` to a 404 — MockMvc verifies the response code and body without needing the real service to throw it
- Security: `@WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN")` tests authorized paths; `mockMvc.perform(get("/admin"))` without auth tests the 401/403 response

**Asserting responses**
- `andExpect(status().isOk())`, `andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(1))`, `andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))` — chain assertions after `perform()`
- For OAuth2 tokens, use `SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt()` or `oidcLogin()` instead of `@WithMockUser`

sections.content:

- **`@Valid` validation is tested here** — send an invalid request body and assert 400 with the right error field names; the service is never called

- **Security with `@WithMockUser` and `jwt()`** — `@WithMockUser(roles="ADMIN")` for role-based tests; `SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt()` for OAuth2/JWT token simulation

sections.title: Choosing the Wrong Test Annotation Adds 10 Seconds Per Test Class — Here's the Decision Tree
sections.content:
Spring Boot provides test annotations that range from loading nothing (`@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`) to loading everything (`@SpringBootTest`). Choosing the right one is the single biggest factor in test suite speed.

The decision tree is simple. Ask: **what am I testing?**

- **Business logic in a service?** → No Spring needed. `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` + `@Mock` + `@InjectMocks`. Runs in milliseconds.
- **Controller request/response mapping?** → `@WebMvcTest(Controller.class)`. Loads web layer only. Runs in ~2 seconds.
- **JPA repository query?** → `@DataJpaTest`. Loads JPA layer with H2 or Testcontainers. Runs in ~3 seconds.
- **JSON serialization?** → `@JsonTest`. Loads Jackson only.
- **REST client behavior?** → `@RestClientTest`. Loads RestTemplate/WebClient with a mock server.
- **Cross-cutting integration?** → `@SpringBootTest`. Full context. 10-30 seconds.

The pattern: **start with the narrowest annotation and widen only if the test requires more context.** If you find yourself adding `@MockBean` for half the beans in a `@SpringBootTest`, you probably need a narrower slice.

sections.title: Test Annotation Decision Matrix
sections.content:
| What you're testing | Annotation | Context size | Startup time | Mock style |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Service business logic | `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension)` | None | <100ms | `@Mock` |
| Controller mapping + validation | `@WebMvcTest` | Web layer | ~2s | `@MockBean` |
| JPA query correctness | `@DataJpaTest` | JPA layer | ~3s | None (real DB) |
| JSON serialization | `@JsonTest` | Jackson only | ~1s | None |
| REST client | `@RestClientTest` | RestTemplate | ~2s | `MockRestServiceServer` |
| Full app integration | `@SpringBootTest` | Everything | 10-30s | `@MockBean` |
| Security rules | `@WebMvcTest` + `@WithMockUser` | Web + Security | ~2s | `@MockBean` |

The startup time column is the hidden cost. 50 test classes using `@SpringBootTest` add 8-25 minutes to CI. The same tests using slices add 2-3 minutes.

sections.title: Context Caching — Why Mock Combinations Matter More Than Test Count
sections.content:
Spring caches the application context and reuses it across test classes with the same configuration. A `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` with `@MockBean UserService` creates one context. A second test class with the same annotation and same `@MockBean` reuses the cached context — zero startup cost.

The cache invalidation happens when the configuration changes: different `@MockBean` sets, different `@TestPropertySource` values, different active profiles. Each unique combination creates a new cache entry and triggers a new context startup.

The practical impact: 10 `@WebMvcTest` classes with the same `@MockBean` service boot ONE context. 10 classes where each mocks a different set of beans boot 10 separate contexts. Standardizing which beans you mock across test classes — using the same base class or consistent mock sets — is the most effective way to speed up a test suite.

Use `--debug` in Surefire/Failsafe to log context cache hits and misses. If you see mostly misses, audit your mock combinations.

sections.title: Real-World Test Suite Structure — How the Pyramid Looks in Code
sections.content:
A well-structured Spring Boot test suite follows a clear directory pattern that mirrors the testing pyramid.

```
src/test/java/com/app/
  unit/           ← @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) — 80% of tests
    service/
    mapper/
    validator/
  integration/    ← @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest — 15% of tests
    controller/
    repository/
  e2e/            ← @SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT) — 5% of tests
    smoke/
    security/
```

The directory structure communicates intent: anything in `unit/` should run without Spring, anything in `integration/` needs a test slice, and `e2e/` needs the full context.

Configure Surefire and Failsafe to run these in stages: unit tests in `mvn test` (Surefire), integration and E2E tests in `mvn verify` (Failsafe). Developers run `mvn test` locally for fast feedback (~30 seconds). CI runs `mvn verify` for full confidence (~3-5 minutes). This separation prevents slow integration tests from blocking the developer's commit cycle.

The 80/15/5 ratio is a guideline, not a rule. Some domains (CRUD apps with little logic) naturally have more integration tests. Complex domains (financial calculations, rule engines) have more unit tests. The ratio should reflect where the complexity lives.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot's test slice annotations let you load only the parts of the context you actually need. The choice of slice is the single biggest factor in test suite speed — a suite that uses `@SpringBootTest` for everything will be 10–50× slower than one using appropriate slices.

**The decision tree**
- No Spring at all: pure unit test with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` — fastest, for business logic in plain classes
- Web layer only: `@WebMvcTest` — controllers, filters, argument resolvers, `@ControllerAdvice`; services must be mocked
- JPA layer only: `@DataJpaTest` — repositories, entity mapping, database queries; service beans are excluded
- Security: `@WebMvcTest` includes security auto-configuration by default — mock the user with `@WithMockUser` or disable specific auto-configurations if testing without security
- Full context: `@SpringBootTest` — smoke tests, full integration flows, application startup verification; not for individual component testing

**Context caching — the hidden optimization**
- Spring caches the ApplicationContext between test classes with identical configuration — if ten `@WebMvcTest` classes all mock the same beans, they share one context; context startup happens once
- Any difference in the set of `@MockBean`, `@TestPropertySource`, or active profiles creates a different cache key — a new context starts
- The optimization: consolidate `@MockBean` declarations in a base test class; all subclasses share the same context because they have identical configuration

**Slices don't load everything**
- `@WebMvcTest` does not load `@Service` or `@Repository` beans — you must `@MockBean` them
- `@DataJpaTest` does not load `@Service` or `@Controller` beans — add `@Import(ConcreteClass.class)` for anything outside the JPA slice

- **`@WebMvcTest` = web layer only** — `@Service` and `@Repository` beans excluded; mock them with `@MockBean`; tests HTTP mapping, validation, security
- **`@DataJpaTest` = JPA layer only** — repositories and entity mapping; services excluded; add `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace=NONE)` for real PostgreSQL via Testcontainers
- **`@SpringBootTest` = full context** — use for smoke tests and full integration paths; not for testing individual components
- **Context caching = the performance trick** — tests with identical `@MockBean` + profile + properties share one context; consolidate mocks in a base class to maximize cache hits

sections.title: A New Container Per Test Class Turns a 3-Second Startup Into a 3-Minute Suite
sections.content:
Testcontainers launches real infrastructure (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch) in Docker containers during tests. The setup is straightforward: declare a container, start it, inject the connection URL, run your tests. The complexity is in **lifecycle management** — specifically, when containers start and stop.

The default pattern (`@Container` on a non-static field) starts a new container for every test method. A static `@Container` starts once per test class. But a test suite with 20 `@DataJpaTest` classes, each starting its own PostgreSQL container, spends 60 seconds just on container startups — the actual tests might take 10 seconds.

The solution is **shared containers across test classes.** Define the container in a base class (or use Testcontainers' reuse feature), start it once for the entire suite, and reuse the same container across all test classes. The container starts in ~3 seconds, the suite runs in ~15 seconds instead of ~75 seconds.

One subtlety: `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions by default, so test isolation is automatic. For containers without transaction support (Redis, Elasticsearch), you need explicit cleanup between tests — `@BeforeEach` with a `flushAll()` or `deleteAll()`.

The container reuse feature (`testcontainers.reuse.enable=true`) is particularly valuable during development. Without reuse, every `mvn test` invocation starts fresh containers. With reuse, the containers persist between runs — your second test run starts instantly. In CI, reuse is typically disabled because each build should start clean. This dual mode (reuse locally, fresh in CI) gives the best of both worlds: fast developer iteration and clean CI verification.

sections.title: The Shared Container Pattern — One Container for All Tests
Best Practices That Prevent Flaky Tests and Slow Suites
sections.content:
**Pin container image versions.** `new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:15.4")` not `"postgres:latest"`. Latest changes without warning, introducing test failures from image updates, not code changes.

**Use `@DynamicPropertySource` over hardcoded ports.** Testcontainers assigns random ports to avoid conflicts. Hardcoding `jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/test` fails when another test or service uses port 5432.

**Pre-pull images in CI.** Container startup includes image download time on first run. Add a CI step that pulls images before running tests: `docker pull postgres:15.4`. This moves the download time out of the test execution.

**Limit container resource usage.** In CI environments with limited resources, set memory limits: `.withCreateContainerCmdModifier(cmd -> cmd.getHostConfig().withMemory(512 * 1024 * 1024))`. A runaway container consuming all CI memory causes all tests to fail.

**Test data isolation matters.** `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions automatically. For Redis tests, call `redisTemplate.getConnectionFactory().getConnection().flushAll()` in `@BeforeEach`. For Elasticsearch, delete and recreate the index. Without cleanup, tests pass individually but fail when run together.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Testcontainers starts real infrastructure — PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch — in Docker containers during your test run. The result is integration tests that run against exactly the same database version, query planner, and SQL dialect as production. H2 can no longer mask production-specific bugs.

**Container lifecycle management**
- `@Container static PostgreSQLContainer<?>` — static means the container starts once when the test class is first loaded and stops when the JVM exits; Ryuk, a cleanup container Testcontainers manages automatically, handles the teardown
- Non-static `@Container` restarts the container for every test method — almost never what you want; startup time multiplies by the number of test methods
- For cross-class sharing: put the container in a base class with `static` scope, or use Testcontainers' singleton pattern where `container.start()` is called in a static initializer

**`@DynamicPropertySource` for Spring integration**

questions.title: Testing Async / CompletableFuture Code
questions.direct_answer: For CompletableFuture, call .get() or .join() in the test to block until the result is available, then assert on it. For @Async Spring methods, either use CountDownLatch/CompletableFuture to wait, or test the underlying method directly without the async wrapper in unit tests. sections.title: Thread.sleep() in Async Tests Is a Bug, Not a Strategy
sections.content:
Testing asynchronous code requires synchronization between the test thread and the async execution. The naive approach — `Thread.sleep(2000)` — is both slow (always waits the full duration) and flaky (fails when execution takes longer than expected on a loaded CI server).

`CompletableFuture` testing is simpler than it appears because the future itself provides the synchronization point. Call `.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` or `.join()` with a timeout — the test blocks until the result is available or times out.

The harder case is testing `@Async` methods in Spring, where the method returns before the async work completes. Here you need an explicit synchronization mechanism: `CountDownLatch`, `Awaitility`, or a `CompletableFuture` that the async code completes. The test waits on this mechanism with a timeout, proceeding as soon as the async work finishes.

The key principle: **every async test needs an explicit synchronization point.** For `CompletableFuture`, the future itself is the synchronization. For `@Async void` methods, you create one — typically by observing a side effect (database write, event, flag). The test waits on this synchronization point with a timeout, never on a fixed sleep duration. Awaitility provides this pattern out of the box with `await().atMost().untilAsserted()`, polling the assertion until it passes or the timeout expires.

How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Testing asynchronous code requires synchronization between the test thread and the async execution. The naive approach — `Thread.sleep(2000)` — is both slow (always waits the full duration even when execution finishes in 50ms) and flaky (fails when the CI server is loaded and execution takes longer than expected).

**Testing `CompletableFuture` directly**
- If your method returns `CompletableFuture<Result>`, call `.get()` in the test — this blocks the test thread until the future completes, gives you the result synchronously, and rethrows exceptions wrapped in `ExecutionException`
- Unwrap `ExecutionException` to test the root cause: `assertThatThrownBy(() -> future.get()).hasCauseInstanceOf(OrderException.class)`
- For timeout testing, use `future.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` — if the future doesn't complete in 5 seconds, the test fails with `TimeoutException` which is informative and deterministic

**Testing `@Async` side effects with Awaitility**
- When `@Async` methods are void (fire and forget), you can't get a return value — the side effect is a database write, a cache update, or an event published
- Awaitility polls a condition until it's true or a timeout is reached: `await().atMost(5, SECONDS).until(() -> orderRepository.count() == 1)`
- This is deterministic — it succeeds as soon as the condition is true, not after a fixed sleep; it fails after the timeout with a meaningful message if the condition is never met

**Exception propagation in `CompletableFuture`**
- Exceptions in `CompletableFuture` chains are wrapped — `future.exceptionally()` handles them inside the chain; `.get()` in tests rethrows them as `ExecutionException`
- `CompletableFuture.get()` vs `join()` — `get()` throws checked `ExecutionException`; `join()` throws unchecked `CompletionException`; in tests, `get()` is more explicit about what you're catching

- **Awaitility for `@Async` side effects** — `await().atMost(5, SECONDS).until(() -> repo.count() == 1)` — polls until true, fails with a clear message if timeout exceeded
- **Exception unwrapping** — `future.get()` throws `ExecutionException`; use `assertThatThrownBy(() -> future.get()).hasCauseInstanceOf(YourException.class)` to assert the root cause

sections.title: Disabling Security in Tests Means You're Not Testing Security — Use @WithMockUser Instead
sections.content:
The instinct when security makes tests fail is to disable it: `@WebMvcTest(excludeAutoConfiguration = SecurityAutoConfiguration.class)`. This makes the tests pass — and completely removes the value of testing that authorized users can access endpoints and unauthorized users cannot.

Spring Security Test provides annotations that create mock authentication without requiring actual login flows. `@WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN")` creates an authenticated user with the ADMIN role. `@WithAnonymousUser` creates an unauthenticated request. These work with both `@WebMvcTest` and `@SpringBootTest` because they inject authentication into Spring Security's context before the request is processed.

The correct approach: **test both the allowed and denied paths.** A security test that only verifies "admin can access" without verifying "user cannot access" proves nothing. The value is in confirming that your security rules accept what they should and reject what they should — testing one side without the other is incomplete.

Spring Security's test support goes beyond simple role checks. `@WithMockUser` handles basic authentication. `@WithSecurityContext` builds custom authentication objects for JWT, OAuth2, or LDAP-based security. `SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt()` creates mock JWT tokens with specific claims and authorities — useful when your security rules depend on JWT claims like `scope`, `tenant_id`, or custom attributes rather than simple roles.

sections.title: Testing Role-Based Access With @WithMockUser
Testing Method-Level Security — @PreAuthorize and @Secured
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The instinct when Spring Security makes tests fail is to disable it. This makes the tests pass — and removes the entire value of testing who can and cannot access your endpoints. Spring Security provides first-class support for testing security rules without disabling them.

**`@WebMvcTest` includes security by default**
- `@WebMvcTest` loads `SecurityAutoConfiguration` — your `@SecurityFilterChain` applies to every MockMvc request; unauthenticated requests to protected endpoints return 401/403, not 200
- To simulate an authenticated user, use `@WithMockUser(username = "alice", roles = "ADMIN")` — sets a `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken` in the `SecurityContext` for the duration of the test
- For method security (`@PreAuthorize`), you need `@EnableMethodSecurity` in the test configuration — `@WebMvcTest` doesn't load it by default

**OAuth2 and JWT testing**
- For JWT-secured endpoints, use `SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt()` — this creates a `JwtAuthenticationToken` with the claims you specify, without a real token or authorization server
- `mockMvc.perform(get("/orders").with(jwt().authorities("SCOPE_orders:read")))` — tests that the endpoint accepts the right scope
- For OIDC, use `SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.oidcLogin()` — creates an `OidcUser` with the attributes and authorities you configure

**Testing unauthorized access**
- Every endpoint test should have an unauthorized scenario — `mockMvc.perform(get("/orders/1"))` without auth should return 401
- Testing the 403 case: authenticate as a user without the required role and assert the response is 403, not 200 — this verifies the authorization rule is actually enforced
- Never use `@WebMvcTest(excludeAutoConfiguration = SecurityAutoConfiguration.class)` — that removes security from the test entirely; the endpoint will return 200 for any request

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Never disable security in tests** — `excludeAutoConfiguration = SecurityAutoConfiguration.class` makes tests pass by removing the thing you're supposed to be testing
- **`@WithMockUser` for role-based tests** — sets a `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken` in `SecurityContext`; tests that the right roles can and cannot access endpoints
- **`jwt()` for OAuth2/JWT** — `SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt().authorities("SCOPE_orders:read")` tests scope enforcement without a real token or authorization server
- **Test both 401 and 403** — unauthenticated request (401) and authenticated-but-wrong-role request (403) are separate scenarios; both must be explicitly tested
- **`@EnableMethodSecurity` must be imported** — `@WebMvcTest` doesn't load it; add it to a test configuration class if you use `@PreAuthorize` annotations

sections.title: 10 Copy-Pasted Test Methods for 10 Inputs Is a Maintenance Nightmare — Parameterize It
sections.content:
When you need to test the same logic with different inputs, the naive approach is copying the test method 10 times and changing the input value. This creates 10 nearly identical methods that must all be updated when the logic changes. `@ParameterizedTest` runs the same test method with different inputs, replacing 10 methods with one.

JUnit 5 provides multiple sources for parameters: `@ValueSource` for single-type primitives, `@CsvSource` for multi-column data, `@EnumSource` for enum values, and `@MethodSource` for complex objects. Each source feeds rows of data into the test method, and JUnit reports each row as a separate test case with a descriptive name.

The real power isn't reducing line count — it's **revealing patterns.** When you see all inputs and expected outputs together, edge cases become visible. Adding a new test case is one line, not copying an entire method. And when the assertion logic changes, you change it in one place.

Beyond reducing code duplication, parameterized tests improve **test documentation.** When all valid and invalid inputs are listed in one place, the test becomes a specification of the method's behavior. A new developer reads the `@CsvSource` or `@MethodSource` and immediately understands all the cases the method handles. Adding a new edge case is one line, not a new method with setup, act, and assert boilerplate. JUnit 5 reports each parameter set as a separate test case, so failures pinpoint the exact failing input without extra debugging.

sections.title: @ValueSource, @CsvSource, and @MethodSource — When to Use Each
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When the same logic needs to be tested with ten different inputs, writing ten near-identical test methods creates ten points of failure when the logic changes. JUnit 5's `@ParameterizedTest` runs the same test method with different inputs from a source you define — eliminating the duplication.

**`@ValueSource` and `@CsvSource` for simple cases**
- `@ValueSource(strings = {"", " ", "null"})` passes each value separately — clean for single-argument tests on simple types
- `@CsvSource({"1, true", "0, false", "-1, false"})` passes multiple arguments as comma-separated rows — each row becomes one test invocation; readable for small datasets
- `@NullAndEmptySource` combined with `@ValueSource` tests null, empty string, and your provided values in one annotation — essential for validation testing

**`@MethodSource` for complex test data**
- `@MethodSource("validOrderCases")` calls a static method that returns a `Stream<Arguments>` — each `Arguments.of(...)` is one test invocation; supports complex objects, not just primitives
- Use `@MethodSource` when test data needs construction logic, when inputs are domain objects, or when you want to give each case a descriptive name
- The static factory method can be in the same test class or in an external class referenced as `"com.example.TestData#validOrderCases"`

**`@EnumSource` for exhaustive enum coverage**
- `@EnumSource(OrderStatus.class)` runs the test once per enum value — guarantees that every status is tested without hardcoding; new enum values automatically get test coverage
- Filter with `@EnumSource(value = OrderStatus.class, names = {"PENDING", "CONFIRMED"})` to test a subset

Display names help identify which case failed — `@ParameterizedTest(name = "order {0} → {1}")` uses the argument values in the failure message.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ParameterizedTest` eliminates copy-paste tests** — one test method, many input cases; when the logic changes, update one place instead of ten
- **`@CsvSource` for small tabular data** — `{"1, true", "0, false"}` — each CSV row is one invocation; readable inline, no separate method needed
- **`@MethodSource` for complex objects** — static factory method returning `Stream<Arguments>`; supports domain objects, nested cases, and descriptive names
- **`@NullAndEmptySource` for validation tests** — tests null and empty string automatically; combine with `@ValueSource` to cover all boundary inputs in one annotation
- **`@EnumSource` for exhaustive coverage** — runs once per enum value; when a new `OrderStatus` is added, it automatically gets tested without touching the test class

sections.title: Kafka Tests Need a Real Broker — @EmbeddedKafka Gives You One Without Docker
sections.content:
Testing Kafka consumers and producers requires a broker. Mocking `KafkaTemplate` tests serialization but misses the actual consume-produce lifecycle — partition assignment, offset management, consumer group coordination. `@EmbeddedKafka` starts an in-memory Kafka broker as part of the Spring test context. No Docker, no external infrastructure.

The embedded broker handles topic creation, partition assignment, and offset tracking exactly like a real broker. Messages sent by `KafkaTemplate` are stored in the embedded broker's log, and `@KafkaListener` instances consume them through the normal consumer group protocol.

The biggest testing mistake is `Thread.sleep()` for synchronization. Kafka consumption is asynchronous — the listener processes messages in a background thread. `Awaitility` or `CountDownLatch` provides proper synchronization that adapts to actual processing speed. A 5-second sleep that "works" locally fails on a loaded CI server where the consumer takes 6 seconds to start.

For teams running many Kafka tests, the embedded broker's startup cost matters. Like Testcontainers, use a shared embedded broker across test classes. Define the `@EmbeddedKafka` configuration in a base class or custom annotation, and Spring's context caching reuses the same broker instance. Different topic configurations invalidate the cache, so standardize topics across test classes where possible.

sections.title: The Full Pattern — Produce, Consume, Assert With Awaitility
Common Pitfalls — Consumer Group Conflicts and Topic Reuse
sections.content:
**Use unique consumer group IDs per test class.** If two test classes share a consumer group ID and run in the same JVM, they compete for partitions. Use `groupId = "test-" + UUID.randomUUID()` or class-specific group IDs.

**Clean up between tests.** The embedded broker persists messages between test methods. If test A sends a message and test B reads from the same topic, test B might see test A's message. Use unique topics per test or clear the consumer's position with `seekToEnd()`.

**Verify error handling, not just happy path.** The highest-value Kafka tests verify that malformed messages reach the DLT, that retries exhaust correctly, and that the consumer continues processing after a failure. These tests catch configuration regressions — someone changes the error handler and the test detects that DLT routing silently broke.

For teams using Testcontainers instead of `@EmbeddedKafka`, the trade-off is startup time vs fidelity. The embedded broker is faster (in-memory) but doesn't support all Kafka features (transactions require specific configuration). Testcontainers' Kafka module runs a real Confluent/Apache Kafka image but adds container startup time.

Another common issue: **serialization configuration in tests must match production.** If your production `KafkaTemplate` uses `JsonSerializer` with specific type mappings, the test template must use the same configuration. A test that sends raw strings but the consumer expects JSON-serialized objects fails with deserialization errors that don't reflect real behavior.

sections.content:
Testing Kafka consumers and producers requires a broker. Mocking KafkaTemplate tests serialization in isolation but misses the actual consume-produce lifecycle. @EmbeddedKafka starts an in-memory Kafka broker as part of the Spring test context, letting you test the full message flow.

**@EmbeddedKafka setup**
- Annotate the test class with @EmbeddedKafka(partitions = 1, topics = {"orders"}) and set @TestPropertySource with spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers=${spring.embedded.kafka.brokers} — the property is set automatically by the embedded broker
- @SpringBootTest is typically needed because you want the full Kafka consumer/producer auto-configuration — @EmbeddedKafka doesn't work well with slices that exclude auto-configuration
- For sending test messages, inject KafkaTemplate and call kafkaTemplate.send("orders", key, payload) — the embedded broker delivers it to your consumer

**Synchronization — the critical part**
- Kafka consumers are asynchronous — the consumer runs in a background thread, not the test thread; Thread.sleep() is unreliable and flaky on loaded CI servers
- Use CountDownLatch inside the listener and latch.await(10, SECONDS) in the test — the listener calls latch.countDown() when it processes a message; the test blocks until that happens
- Awaitility is cleaner: await().atMost(10, SECONDS).until(() -> processedMessages.size() == 1) — polls until the consumer has processed the message

**Testcontainers Kafka as the alternative**
- @EmbeddedKafka is fast and simple but runs a simplified implementation — some production behaviors like SSL, ACLs, and replication are not faithfully reproduced
- Testcontainers Kafka runs a real Confluent Platform or Apache Kafka image in Docker — slower startup but catches issues the embedded broker misses
- Use @EmbeddedKafka for fast consumer/producer tests; Testcontainers Kafka for integration tests that validate real Kafka configuration

sections.content:

- **Thread.sleep() is wrong for consumer tests** — consumers run on background threads; use CountDownLatch.await() or Awaitility to synchronize deterministically
- **CountDownLatch pattern** — inject a latch into the listener, call latch.countDown() when a message is processed, latch.await(10, SECONDS) in the test
- **Testcontainers Kafka for real configuration** — SSL, ACLs, partition replication; the embedded broker doesn't reproduce these; use real Kafka in Docker for configuration validation
- **@SpringBootTest is usually required** — @EmbeddedKafka needs full auto-configuration for Kafka consumers and producers to wire correctly

questions.question: What is Test-Driven Development (TDD) and how does the red-green-refactor cycle work in practice?
questions.title: Test-Driven Development: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle
questions.direct_answer: TDD is a development practice where you write a failing test before writing the production code. The cycle is: Red — write the smallest possible failing test. Green — write the minimum production code to make it pass. Refactor — clean up the code while keeping all tests green. Benefits include built-in test coverage, emergent design, and a safety net for future changes. The key discipline is writing the minimal code to pass each test, then improving it in the refactor phase.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you have actually practised TDD and understand the discipline it requires, not just the theory
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing the full production implementation before any tests and calling it TDD — true TDD requires the test to drive the design, which often leads to better API design than implementation-first
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss how TDD naturally leads to testable, loosely coupled design because code that is hard to test in isolation is a design smell; and distinguish TDD from test coverage as a metric

sections.title: TDD Isn't About Testing — It's About Designing Code Through Usage Before Implementation
sections.content:
Test-Driven Development means writing the test **before** the production code. The cycle is red-green-refactor: write a failing test (red), write the minimum code to make it pass (green), then improve the code without changing behavior (refactor).

The common misconception is that TDD is a testing technique. It's actually a **design technique.** By writing the test first, you're forced to think about the public API before the implementation — what arguments does the method take? What does it return? What exceptions does it throw? The test becomes a specification of behavior, and the code is written to satisfy that specification.

The biggest mistake is writing the full implementation first and calling it TDD because tests exist. TDD's value comes from the **sequence**: the test drives the design. When you write the implementation first, the test validates what you already built — it doesn't shape the API or catch design problems early.

TDD works best for **business logic and domain code** — services, validators, calculators, state machines. It's less useful for wiring code (controllers, configuration) where the design is dictated by frameworks. Don't force TDD on code where the test would just verify that you called Spring's API correctly.

sections.title: Red-Green-Refactor — A Concrete Walk-Through
When TDD Helps vs When It Gets in the Way
sections.content:
**TDD works best for:**
- Business logic with clear inputs and outputs (calculators, validators, transformers)
- Domain models with state transitions (order lifecycle, approval workflows)
- Algorithms with known edge cases (parsing, formatting, search)
- Bug fixes — write a test that reproduces the bug first, then fix it; the test prevents regression

**TDD is less useful for:**
- CRUD controllers where the design is dictated by the framework
- Configuration classes where the test would just verify Spring wiring
- UI code where behavior depends on visual rendering
- Exploratory prototyping where the API is still being discovered

The practical compromise: use TDD for domain logic and service layers. Write tests after for controllers, repositories, and integration points. The goal is confident, well-designed code — not dogmatic adherence to a process. A team that writes excellent tests after implementation is better off than a team that writes poor tests before it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Test-Driven Development means writing the test before the production code. The cycle is red-green-refactor: write a failing test, write the minimum code to make it pass, then improve the code without changing behavior. The common misconception is that TDD is a testing technique — it is a design technique.

**What the cycle forces**
- Red: writing the test before the code means you must define the API — method signature, parameter types, return type, exception contract — before deciding how to implement it; the test is the first client of your design
- Green: write the minimum code to make the test pass — not the complete implementation, just enough; this prevents over-engineering and keeps each increment small and verifiable
- Refactor: improve the code structure — extract methods, rename, eliminate duplication — without changing any observable behavior; the passing tests are your safety net

**TDD as a design technique**
- Code that is hard to test in isolation usually has too many responsibilities or too many hidden dependencies — TDD reveals this immediately because you must instantiate the class and define its collaborators before writing a single assertion
- If creating a test requires mocking ten dependencies, that is a design smell TDD surfaced — not a testing problem; the class has too many concerns
- Classes that emerge from TDD tend to be small, single-purpose, and dependency-injected — because the test requires clean construction

**When TDD pays off vs when it is overhead**
- High-value: complex business rules with many edge cases, algorithmic code where correctness matters, code that will be modified frequently
- Lower-value: UI code, infrastructure configuration, simple CRUD with no logic, exploratory prototypes — write the code first and test after
- TDD does not mean 100% coverage — it means letting tests drive the design; coverage is a side effect, not the goal

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **TDD = design technique, not testing technique** — the test is written first to define the API; writing tests after is not TDD even if tests exist
- **Red = specification** — define method signature, parameter types, return type, and expected behavior before any production code; the test is the contract
- **Green = minimum code** — just enough to pass the failing test; no premature generalization; the next test drives the next requirement
- **Refactor = design improvement** — improve structure with all tests passing as the safety net; never skip the refactor step
- **Hard to test = design signal** — if setup requires five mocks, the class has too many responsibilities; TDD surfaced a design problem, not a testing problem

sections.title: Mockito Gives You Three Capabilities — Stubbing, Verification, and Argument Capture
sections.content:
Most developers learn `when().thenReturn()` and stop. But Mockito has three distinct capabilities that serve different testing needs, and using the wrong one weakens your tests.

**Stubbing** (`when().thenReturn()`) controls what the mock returns. This is input to the code under test — you set up the world the code will see.

**Verification** (`verify()`) confirms the code under test called a dependency with expected arguments. This is output validation — did the service actually call the repository's `save()` method? Did it call the notification client?

**Argument capture** (`ArgumentCaptor`) grabs the actual object passed to a mock method so you can assert on its fields. This bridges the gap between stubbing (what goes in) and verification (what comes out) — it tells you *exactly what was passed* to a dependency.

The distinction matters because each serves a different testing purpose. Stubbing sets up preconditions. Verification confirms side effects. Argument capture validates the data flow between components. A well-written unit test often uses all three: stub the repository to return test data, verify the email service was called, and capture the email to assert it has the right subject and recipient.

sections.title: verify() — Testing Interactions, Not Just Return Values
ArgumentCaptor — When verify() Isn't Enough
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Mockito's when().thenReturn() is just one capability. The library has three distinct concepts — stubbing, verification, and argument capture — that serve different testing needs. Using only stubbing and ignoring verify and ArgumentCaptor means your tests can pass even when code calls the wrong methods with wrong arguments.

**Stubbing — controlling what collaborators return**
- when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(order)) sets up what the mock returns for a specific input; the test then exercises the code that depends on this return value
- For void methods, use doThrow(new RuntimeException()).when(repo).delete(any()) — when().thenReturn() does not work with void return types
- For spies, always use doReturn().when() syntax — when().thenReturn() calls the real method first before applying the stub, causing unexpected side effects

**verify() — proving interactions happened**
- verify(emailSender).send(any(Email.class)) asserts the mock method was called at least once; verify(emailSender, times(2)) for exact count; verify(emailSender, never()) for zero calls
- Use verify() when the behavior you are testing is a side effect — the method returns void but is supposed to call something; the assertion is on the interaction, not a return value
- Over-verification is a test smell: verifying every internal call makes tests break on every refactor even when behavior is unchanged; verify externally observable interactions only

**ArgumentCaptor — asserting what was passed**
- ArgumentCaptor<Email> captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Email.class) — after calling verify(emailSender).send(captor.capture()), captor.getValue() gives you the actual Email object that was passed
- Use this when the argument is constructed inside the method under test and you need to assert its properties — the only alternative would be a complex matcher
- BDD-style aliases: given().willReturn() instead of when().thenReturn(), then(mock).should() instead of verify() — same behavior, reads like a test scenario

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Stubbing = what collaborators return** — when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(order)); use doThrow() for void methods; use doReturn().when() for spies
- **verify() = prove interactions happened** — verify(emailSender, times(1)).send(any()) asserts a side-effect call occurred; use when the behavior is a call, not a return value
- **ArgumentCaptor = assert what was passed** — capture the argument to a void method and assert its properties; needed when the argument is constructed inside the method under test
- **Over-verification is a smell** — verifying every internal call makes tests brittle on refactoring; verify only externally observable behavior
- **doReturn().when() for spies** — when(spy.method()).thenReturn() calls the real method first; doReturn().when(spy).method() stubs without invoking the real implementation

questions.title: Integration Testing in Spring Boot — @SpringBootTest, @DataJpaTest, @WebMvcTest

sections.title: @SpringBootTest Loads Everything — That's Why It's Slow and Why Slices Exist
sections.content:
`@SpringBootTest` starts the full Spring application context — every bean, every auto-configuration, every component scan. This gives maximum fidelity but at a cost: context startup takes 5-30 seconds depending on the application. For a project with 200 tests all using `@SpringBootTest`, the test suite runs for 30+ minutes.

**Test slices** load only the parts of the context relevant to what you're testing. `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` loads the web layer — controller, filters, converters — but not services, repositories, or database connections. `@DataJpaTest` loads JPA repositories and an embedded H2 database but not controllers or services.

The performance difference is dramatic. A `@WebMvcTest` starts in under 2 seconds. The same test with `@SpringBootTest` takes 10-15 seconds because it loads the entire application including database connections, message brokers, and scheduled tasks that the test doesn't need.

Spring caches application contexts across tests with the same configuration — but slices with different `@MockBean` annotations create different cache keys, triggering new context creation. Minimizing distinct `@MockBean` combinations across test classes keeps context caching effective.

sections.title: Test Slice Selection — What Each Annotation Loads
sections.content:
| Annotation | What it loads | What it excludes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@SpringBootTest` | Everything | Nothing | Full integration tests, app startup verification |
| `@WebMvcTest` | Controllers, filters, `@ControllerAdvice` | Services, repositories, DB | Controller request/response testing |
| `@DataJpaTest` | JPA repos, `EntityManager`, H2/Testcontainers | Controllers, services | Repository query verification |
| `@WebFluxTest` | WebFlux controllers | Everything else | Reactive controller testing |
| `@JsonTest` | Jackson `ObjectMapper` | Everything else | JSON serialization/deserialization |
| `@RestClientTest` | `RestTemplate` / `WebClient` with mock server | Everything else | External API client testing |

The pattern: **use the narrowest slice that covers what you're testing.** If you're testing a controller's request mapping and validation, `@WebMvcTest` is faster and more focused than `@SpringBootTest`. If you're testing a JPA query, `@DataJpaTest` loads only what the repository needs.

sections.title: When @SpringBootTest Is Actually the Right Choice
Test Profile and Property Overrides — Isolating Test Configuration
sections.content:
Test slices often need different configuration than production. `@TestPropertySource(properties = "spring.jpa.show-sql=true")` overrides individual properties. `@ActiveProfiles("test")` activates a test-specific `application-test.yml` with test database URLs, disabled scheduling, and mock external service endpoints.

The hierarchy matters: `@TestPropertySource` overrides profile properties, which override `application.yml`. This lets you keep most configuration in the default file and override only what's test-specific.

One pattern that prevents test configuration drift: create a `src/test/resources/application-test.yml` that disables everything tests don't need — scheduled tasks (`spring.task.scheduling.enabled=false`), actuator endpoints, and Kafka auto-configuration. Tests start faster because Spring skips auto-configuration for components that aren't part of the test.

For `@DataJpaTest`, properties like `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop` ensure a clean schema per test run. Combined with `@Transactional` rollback, this gives complete test isolation without manual cleanup scripts.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Integration testing in Spring Boot covers a spectrum from targeted slice tests to full context tests. The most common mistake is using @SpringBootTest for every integration test — it is the slowest option and usually unnecessary for what you are actually testing.

**@SpringBootTest — the full assembly**
- Loads the entire application context — every bean, every auto-configuration, every component; provides maximum confidence that the application assembles correctly
- Use for smoke tests where the app starts, cross-cutting configuration where security plus caching plus transactions all interact, and full E2E flows through the entire stack
- Pair with @AutoConfigureMockMvc for HTTP tests or @AutoConfigureWebTestClient for reactive applications
- Context caching: Spring reuses the context between test classes with identical configuration; @MockBean variations break the cache — consolidate them in base classes

**The slice strategy**
- @WebMvcTest loads the web layer — controllers, filters, exception handlers; mock services with @MockBean; fast, targeted, millisecond startup
- @DataJpaTest loads JPA and repositories; add @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE) with Testcontainers for real database testing
- @DataRedisTest loads Redis repositories and caching; needs a real Redis instance or Testcontainers
- Combine slices with @Import to pull in specific beans outside the slice default scope

**@MockBean and context cache invalidation**
- Each unique set of @MockBean declarations creates a separate cached context — test class A with one mock and class B with two mocks are different cache keys; new contexts load for each
- The fix: a base test class declaring all the mocks that a category of tests needs — all subclasses share the same cache entry and Spring starts the context only once

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@SpringBootTest = full assembly** — use for smoke tests and cross-cutting configuration; not for testing individual service or controller behavior
- **Slice tests are faster** — @WebMvcTest for controllers, @DataJpaTest for repositories; each loads only what the component under test needs
- **Context caching = the performance multiplier** — tests with identical configuration share one context; consolidate @MockBean declarations in a base class to maximize cache hits

sections.title: A New Container Per Test Class Turns a 3-Second Startup Into a 3-Minute Suite
sections.content:
Testcontainers launches real infrastructure (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch) in Docker containers during tests. The setup is straightforward: declare a container, start it, inject the connection URL, run your tests. The complexity is in **lifecycle management** — specifically, when containers start and stop.

The default pattern (`@Container` on a non-static field) starts a new container for every test method. A static `@Container` starts once per test class. But a test suite with 20 `@DataJpaTest` classes, each starting its own PostgreSQL container, spends 60 seconds just on container startups — the actual tests might take 10 seconds.

The solution is **shared containers across test classes.** Define the container in a base class (or use Testcontainers' reuse feature), start it once for the entire suite, and reuse the same container across all test classes. The container starts in ~3 seconds, the suite runs in ~15 seconds instead of ~75 seconds.

One subtlety: `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions by default, so test isolation is automatic. For containers without transaction support (Redis, Elasticsearch), you need explicit cleanup between tests — `@BeforeEach` with a `flushAll()` or `deleteAll()`.

The container reuse feature (`testcontainers.reuse.enable=true`) is particularly valuable during development. Without reuse, every `mvn test` invocation starts fresh containers. With reuse, the containers persist between runs — your second test run starts instantly. In CI, reuse is typically disabled because each build should start clean. This dual mode (reuse locally, fresh in CI) gives the best of both worlds: fast developer iteration and clean CI verification.

sections.title: The Shared Container Pattern — One Container for All Tests
Best Practices That Prevent Flaky Tests and Slow Suites
sections.content:
**Pin container image versions.** `new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:15.4")` not `"postgres:latest"`. Latest changes without warning, introducing test failures from image updates, not code changes.

**Use `@DynamicPropertySource` over hardcoded ports.** Testcontainers assigns random ports to avoid conflicts. Hardcoding `jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/test` fails when another test or service uses port 5432.

**Pre-pull images in CI.** Container startup includes image download time on first run. Add a CI step that pulls images before running tests: `docker pull postgres:15.4`. This moves the download time out of the test execution.

**Limit container resource usage.** In CI environments with limited resources, set memory limits: `.withCreateContainerCmdModifier(cmd -> cmd.getHostConfig().withMemory(512 * 1024 * 1024))`. A runaway container consuming all CI memory causes all tests to fail.

**Test data isolation matters.** `@DataJpaTest` rolls back transactions automatically. For Redis tests, call `redisTemplate.getConnectionFactory().getConnection().flushAll()` in `@BeforeEach`. For Elasticsearch, delete and recreate the index. Without cleanup, tests pass individually but fail when run together.

Testcontainers starts real Docker containers — PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka — during your test run. Integration tests run against exactly the same infrastructure version, query planner, and SQL dialect as production. H2 can no longer hide production-specific failures.

- @Container static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres starts once when the test class loads and stops when the JVM exits; Ryuk, a cleanup container Testcontainers manages automatically, handles teardown

- Containers get dynamically assigned ports — you cannot hardcode the JDBC URL; @DynamicPropertySource runs before Spring creates the context and injects the actual runtime values

- Required alongside @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE) when using @DataJpaTest — otherwise Spring replaces the DataSource with H2 regardless of your Testcontainers setup

**Container reuse for development speed**
- Testcontainers reuse mode with withReuse(true) keeps the container running between test suite executions — the second run skips Docker container startup entirely
- Ryuk automatically tears down containers when the JVM exits — even if the test crashes, containers do not accumulate on the host
- DockerComposeContainer is available for multi-service tests that need PostgreSQL plus Redis plus Kafka simultaneously
