sections.title: MockMvc Tests the Controller Layer Without Starting a Server — That's Both Its Power and Its Limitation
sections.content:
MockMvc simulates HTTP requests through Spring's `DispatcherServlet` without starting a real HTTP server. No socket binding, no TCP overhead — requests go directly through the servlet pipeline. This makes controller tests fast (milliseconds) while still exercising the full Spring MVC stack: request mapping, parameter binding, validation, exception handling, and content negotiation.

The limitation: MockMvc bypasses the HTTP transport layer. Issues that only appear with a real server — CORS configuration, SSL, response compression, multipart parsing edge cases — won't be caught. For these, you need `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` with `TestRestTemplate`.

MockMvc pairs best with `@WebMvcTest`, which loads only the controller layer. Dependencies like services and repositories are mocked with `@MockBean`. This combination tests that your controller correctly maps requests, validates input, calls the right service method, and returns the right HTTP status and response body — without touching the database or any real service.

The key advantage of MockMvc over a real HTTP test: **speed and determinism.** No port binding, no network stack, no race conditions from async startup. A MockMvc test suite with 50 controller tests runs in under 5 seconds because the servlet simulation has zero network overhead. This makes it practical to test every request mapping, every validation rule, and every error response without slowing down the developer feedback loop.

sections.title: Testing Request Mapping, Validation, and Error Handling in One Test
Testing Error Responses, Security, and Custom Argument Resolvers
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MockMvc tests your REST controllers through Spring DispatcherServlet without starting an HTTP server. Requests go directly through the servlet pipeline — request mapping, argument resolution, validation, and exception handling all execute exactly as in production, but without network overhead.

**Setup — @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest**
- @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) is the right choice — loads only the web layer, mock services with @MockBean, runs in milliseconds; this is the preferred approach for isolated controller testing
- @SpringBootTest with @AutoConfigureMockMvc loads the full context — slower, but gives real service behavior when you need integration-style controller tests
- Standalone setup with MockMvcBuilders.standaloneSetup requires manual configuration of every @ControllerAdvice, argument resolver, and filter — tedious and easy to miss something

**Testing the complete HTTP contract**
- Request mapping: perform(get("/orders/1")) verifies path variables bind correctly and the right controller method executes
- Request validation: perform(post("/orders").contentType(APPLICATION_JSON).content("{}")) triggers @Valid violations and produces a 400 with the expected error body shape
- Exception handling: stub the service to throw OrderNotFoundException; assert MockMvc returns 404 with the error JSON your @ControllerAdvice produces
- Security: @WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN") tests authorized access; perform without auth tests the 401 or 403 response

**Asserting responses**
- andExpect(status().isOk()) for HTTP status; andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(1)) for specific JSON fields; andExpect(content().contentType(APPLICATION_JSON)) for headers
- andDo(print()) prints the full request and response to stdout during debugging — invaluable when an assertion fails and you need to see the actual response

- **Test exception mapping** — stub the service to throw a domain exception; assert @ControllerAdvice produces the right status code and error JSON shape
- **Security included by default** — @WebMvcTest loads SecurityAutoConfiguration; use @WithMockUser or jwt() post-processor for authenticated requests; test 401 and 403 explicitly

questions.question: Test-Driven Development (TDD) — Red-Green-Refactor in Java
questions.title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) — Red-Green-Refactor in Java
questions.direct_answer: TDD means writing a failing test first, implementing the minimum to pass it, then refactoring. The test drives API design before implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands TDD's red-green-refactor cycle and when it adds value.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing full implementation first and claiming TDD because tests exist.

sections.title: TDD Isn't About Testing — It's About Designing Code Through Usage Before Implementation
sections.content:
Test-Driven Development means writing the test **before** the production code. The cycle is red-green-refactor: write a failing test (red), write the minimum code to make it pass (green), then improve the code without changing behavior (refactor).

The common misconception is that TDD is a testing technique. It's actually a **design technique.** By writing the test first, you're forced to think about the public API before the implementation — what arguments does the method take? What does it return? What exceptions does it throw? The test becomes a specification of behavior, and the code is written to satisfy that specification.

The biggest mistake is writing the full implementation first and calling it TDD because tests exist. TDD's value comes from the **sequence**: the test drives the design. When you write the implementation first, the test validates what you already built — it doesn't shape the API or catch design problems early.

TDD works best for **business logic and domain code** — services, validators, calculators, state machines. It's less useful for wiring code (controllers, configuration) where the design is dictated by frameworks. Don't force TDD on code where the test would just verify that you called Spring's API correctly.

sections.title: Red-Green-Refactor — A Concrete Walk-Through
When TDD Helps vs When It Gets in the Way
sections.content:
**TDD works best for:**
- Business logic with clear inputs and outputs (calculators, validators, transformers)
- Domain models with state transitions (order lifecycle, approval workflows)
- Algorithms with known edge cases (parsing, formatting, search)
- Bug fixes — write a test that reproduces the bug first, then fix it; the test prevents regression

**TDD is less useful for:**
- CRUD controllers where the design is dictated by the framework
- Configuration classes where the test would just verify Spring wiring
- UI code where behavior depends on visual rendering
- Exploratory prototyping where the API is still being discovered

The practical compromise: use TDD for domain logic and service layers. Write tests after for controllers, repositories, and integration points. The goal is confident, well-designed code — not dogmatic adherence to a process. A team that writes excellent tests after implementation is better off than a team that writes poor tests before it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Test-Driven Development is a discipline, not just a testing technique. The cycle — write a failing test, make it pass, refactor — forces design decisions before implementation decisions. The test is the first client of your API, and writing it first means you think about usability before you think about internals.

**The three steps and what each forces**
- Red: you define the class name, method signature, parameter types, return type, and expected behavior before writing a single line of production code — the test is your specification, not an afterthought
- Green: write just enough code to pass the test — no premature generalization, no handling of cases the test does not cover yet; the next test drives the next increment of implementation
- Refactor: improve the code — extract methods, rename variables, eliminate duplication — without breaking any test; this is when you clean up the minimal green code

**TDD reveals design problems early**
- A class that requires creating five mock objects before you can write a single assertion has too many responsibilities — TDD surfaces this before the class is entrenched in the codebase
- A method whose behavior cannot be specified in a test without intimate knowledge of internals is poorly encapsulated — TDD forces you to design from the outside in
- Classes that emerge from TDD tend to be small, focused, and dependency-injected because the test requires clean construction

**Where TDD makes sense vs where it is overhead**
- Makes sense: complex domain logic with edge cases, algorithmic code, code that has been defect-prone, public APIs that need a clear contract defined up front
- Overhead: infrastructure configuration, UI code, exploratory prototypes, trivial CRUD — write the code first and test after in these cases
- TDD does not mean 100% coverage — it means letting tests drive the design; coverage is a side effect of well-driven development, not the goal

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **TDD = design technique** — the test written first forces API design before implementation; writing tests after is not TDD even if coverage is high
- **Red = specification** — define method signature, parameter types, return type, and expected behavior before any production code exists
- **Green = minimum code** — just enough to pass the failing test; no premature generalization; the next test drives the next requirement
- **Refactor = design improvement** — improve structure with all tests as the safety net; never skip the refactor step
- **Hard to test = design signal** — if setup requires five mocks, the class has too many responsibilities; TDD revealed a design problem, not a testing problem

questions.question: Code Coverage with JaCoCo — What to Measure and What to Ignore
questions.title: Code Coverage with JaCoCo — What to Measure and What to Ignore
questions.direct_answer: JaCoCo measures how much code is executed during tests. Line coverage counts executed lines. Branch coverage counts executed decision paths. Coverage measures test execution, not test quality.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands what code coverage measures, its limitations, and what coverage targets are meaningful.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Chasing 100% coverage by testing getters, setters, and trivial code — this adds test maintenance cost without catching bugs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain branch coverage vs line coverage, why coverage targets should differ by code type (80%+ for business logic, lower for configuration), and how JaCoCo exclusions prevent misleading metrics.

sections.title: 100% Coverage Doesn't Mean Zero Bugs — It Means Every Line Was Executed, Not Verified
sections.content:
Code coverage measures what percentage of your code runs during tests. **Line coverage** counts lines executed. **Branch coverage** counts decision paths taken — both the `if` and `else` branches. JaCoCo is the standard coverage tool for Java projects, integrated into Maven/Gradle and CI pipelines.

The misconception: high coverage = good tests. A test that calls every method but asserts nothing has 100% coverage and catches zero bugs. Coverage measures **execution, not verification.** A line is "covered" if it ran during any test, regardless of whether the test checked the output.

The practical target: **80% line coverage for business logic, lower for configuration and boilerplate.** Chasing 100% means testing getters, setters, generated code, and exception paths that add maintenance cost without catching bugs. The last 20% of coverage typically requires 80% of the testing effort — and that effort is better spent on edge cases in critical code than on covering trivial code.

Branch coverage is more valuable than line coverage. A method with an `if/else` can have 100% line coverage (both branches run) but if you only test the `true` branch, you miss bugs in the `false` path. JaCoCo tracks both and reports them separately.

sections.title: Configuring JaCoCo With Meaningful Exclusions
sections.content:
JaCoCo integrates with Maven via the `jacoco-maven-plugin`. The key configuration is **exclusions** — removing code that shouldn't affect your coverage metric.

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
    <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <excludes>
            <exclude>**/config/**</exclude>
            <exclude>**/dto/**</exclude>
            <exclude>**/*Application.class</exclude>
            <exclude>**/generated/**</exclude>
        </excludes>
    </configuration>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals>
        </execution>
        <execution>
            <id>report</id>
            <phase>verify</phase>
            <goals><goal>report</goal></goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

Exclude configuration classes (pure Spring wiring), DTOs (data carriers with no logic), the main application class, and generated code (MapStruct, Lombok). Without exclusions, these inflate your coverage denominator — making it harder to reach meaningful coverage targets for actual business logic.

For enforcement, add a `check` goal with `BUNDLE` rules: `LINE` minimum 0.80, `BRANCH` minimum 0.70. JaCoCo fails the build if coverage drops below the threshold. Set thresholds per package if different areas have different complexity levels.

sections.title: What to Measure and What to Ignore — The Coverage Strategy
sections.content:
**High coverage targets (80%+):** business logic services, domain models, validators, calculators. This is where bugs live and where tests provide the most value. Branch coverage matters here — every `if/else` decision path should be tested.

**Moderate coverage (60-80%):** controllers, mappers, integration code. These are mostly wiring — the framework does most of the work. Test the important paths (validation, error handling) but don't force coverage on trivial mappings.

**Low or excluded:** configuration classes, DTOs, generated code, the main class. Testing `@Bean` definitions and data carriers adds maintenance cost without catching bugs.

The coverage report should be a conversation tool, not a gate. A team that discusses uncovered branches in code review catches more bugs than a team that mandates 90% coverage and writes `@Test void testGetters()` to hit the number.

One metric worth tracking: **coverage of changed code.** CI tools like SonarQube measure "coverage on new code" separately. Requiring 80% coverage on new code is more effective than requiring 80% overall — it ensures new features are tested without forcing retroactive testing of legacy code.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Code coverage measures what percentage of your code executes during tests. JaCoCo is the standard tool for Java — it integrates with Maven and Gradle, generates HTML reports, and can enforce minimum thresholds that fail the build. But chasing percentages is the wrong goal.

**Line coverage vs branch coverage**
- Line coverage counts whether a line was executed at least once — a test that calls process(validInput) covers every line in the happy path but misses null handling, exception paths, and edge cases
- Branch coverage requires both sides of every conditional to be exercised — both the if and else of every decision; this is more meaningful because it catches untested decision paths
- JaCoCo reports both; configure minimum thresholds in build config; branch coverage around 70-80% for business logic is more meaningful than 100% line coverage

**What to cover vs what to exclude**
- High-value targets: business logic, validation rules, service methods, domain objects — these are where bugs live; aim for 80%+ branch coverage
- Exclude from coverage: Spring configuration classes, generated code, JPA entity getters and setters, Lombok-generated code, @SpringBootApplication main class
- JaCoCo exclusions: @ExcludeFromJacocoGeneratedReport on methods or classes, or regex patterns in the JaCoCo configuration for package-level exclusions

**The 100% trap**
- 100% coverage does not mean zero bugs — you can cover every line with tests that make no meaningful assertions; coverage tells you code was executed, not that it was verified correctly

sections.title: assertEquals Tells You It Failed — AssertJ Tells You Why
sections.content:
JUnit 5's built-in assertions (`assertEquals`, `assertTrue`, `assertThrows`) work but produce minimal failure messages. `assertEquals(3, list.size())` fails with "expected 3 but was 5" — but doesn't tell you what was in the list. You add a message parameter, but now every assertion is two lines of boilerplate.

AssertJ's fluent API solves both readability and failure messages: `assertThat(list).hasSize(3)` fails with "Expected size: 3 but was: 5 in: [item1, item2, item3, item4, item5]" — showing the actual content. The assertion reads like a sentence, and the failure message includes context you'd otherwise need to add manually.

AssertJ is not a replacement for JUnit 5 — it's a complement. JUnit handles test lifecycle (`@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, `@ParameterizedTest`). AssertJ handles assertions. Together, they give you the test structure of JUnit and the assertion expressiveness of a dedicated library.

The key advantage: **method chains.** `assertThat(user).isNotNull().extracting(User::getName, User::getEmail).containsExactly("John", "john@test.com")` replaces three separate assertions with one fluent chain. Each chained method narrows the assertion, and any failure shows exactly which condition failed.

sections.title: Collection and Exception Assertions — Where AssertJ Shines Brightest
sections.content:
Collection assertions are where AssertJ's value is most obvious.

```java
assertThat(orders)
    .hasSize(3)
    .extracting(Order::getStatus)
    .containsExactlyInAnyOrder(Status.PENDING, Status.SHIPPED, Status.DELIVERED);

assertThat(users)
    .filteredOn(User::isActive, true)
    .extracting(User::getEmail)
    .contains("active@test.com")
    .doesNotContain("inactive@test.com");
```

`extracting()` pulls a field from each element, turning a `List<Order>` into a list of statuses for easier assertion. `filteredOn()` subsets the collection inline. Compare this to JUnit: you'd need a stream, a collect, and separate assertions.

Exception assertions are equally clean:

```java
assertThatThrownBy(() -> userService.findById(999L))
    .isInstanceOf(UserNotFoundException.class)
    .hasMessage("User 999 not found")
    .hasFieldOrPropertyWithValue("userId", 999L);
```

This replaces JUnit's `assertThrows` + separate message assertion with one fluent chain. The `hasFieldOrPropertyWithValue` check inspects exception fields — useful for custom exceptions with context data.

sections.title: Soft Assertions — Reporting All Failures at Once
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JUnit 5 ships with built-in assertions — assertEquals, assertTrue, assertThrows — that work but produce poor failure messages. assertEquals(3, list.size()) fails with "expected 3 but was 5" without showing what was actually in the list. AssertJ's fluent API gives failure messages that diagnose the problem without needing a debugger.

**AssertJ fluent API basics**
- assertThat(order.status()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.CONFIRMED) reads like English and produces "expected: CONFIRMED but was: PENDING" on failure — the type is shown, the comparison is explicit
- assertThat(orders).hasSize(3).extracting(Order::id).containsExactly(1L, 2L, 3L) chains assertions on collections; failure shows the actual list content, not just the size discrepancy
- assertThat(result).isPresent().get().satisfies(o -> assertThat(o.total()).isGreaterThan(BigDecimal.ZERO)) handles Optional unwrapping with a nested assertion in one expression

**Exception assertions with AssertJ**
- assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.process(null)).isInstanceOf(ValidationException.class).hasMessageContaining("required") — type, message, and cause chain in one fluent expression
- Cleaner than JUnit 5's assertThrows for checking exception message, cause, and type together in a single readable assertion
- assertThatCode(() -> service.process(valid)).doesNotThrowAnyException() — positive assertion that no exception is thrown; clearer than an empty test with no exception assertion

**Soft assertions — collecting all failures**
- SoftAssertions.assertSoftly runs all assertions even if the first fails; the report shows every problem at once instead of stopping at the first failure

**Custom assertions**
- Extend AbstractAssert to create assertThat(order).isConfirmed().hasPositiveTotal() in domain language; tests become readable specifications for your domain model

sections.title: 10 Copy-Pasted Test Methods for 10 Inputs Is a Maintenance Nightmare — Parameterize It
sections.content:
When you need to test the same logic with different inputs, the naive approach is copying the test method 10 times and changing the input value. This creates 10 nearly identical methods that must all be updated when the logic changes. `@ParameterizedTest` runs the same test method with different inputs, replacing 10 methods with one.

JUnit 5 provides multiple sources for parameters: `@ValueSource` for single-type primitives, `@CsvSource` for multi-column data, `@EnumSource` for enum values, and `@MethodSource` for complex objects. Each source feeds rows of data into the test method, and JUnit reports each row as a separate test case with a descriptive name.

The real power isn't reducing line count — it's **revealing patterns.** When you see all inputs and expected outputs together, edge cases become visible. Adding a new test case is one line, not copying an entire method. And when the assertion logic changes, you change it in one place.

Beyond reducing code duplication, parameterized tests improve **test documentation.** When all valid and invalid inputs are listed in one place, the test becomes a specification of the method's behavior. A new developer reads the `@CsvSource` or `@MethodSource` and immediately understands all the cases the method handles. Adding a new edge case is one line, not a new method with setup, act, and assert boilerplate. JUnit 5 reports each parameter set as a separate test case, so failures pinpoint the exact failing input without extra debugging.

sections.title: @ValueSource, @CsvSource, and @MethodSource — When to Use Each
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Parameterized tests eliminate the copy-paste problem — when the same logic needs verification against many inputs, @ParameterizedTest runs one method with a stream of arguments instead of requiring one method per input case.

**@ValueSource and @NullAndEmptySource for simple types**
- @ValueSource(ints = {1, 5, 100}) passes each int separately; @ValueSource(strings = {"alice", "bob"}) for strings — clean for single-argument tests on primitives and strings
- @NullAndEmptySource tests null and empty string as separate cases — essential for validation tests where both must be rejected
- Combine them: @NullAndEmptySource @ValueSource(strings = {" ", "	"}) runs four cases covering null, empty, space, and tab in one annotation pair

**@CsvSource for multiple arguments**
- Each string in @CsvSource is one test case with comma-separated values — {"1, 100.0, PENDING", "2, 0.0, INVALID"} passes id, amount, and expected status as three arguments
- Add nullValues = "NULL" to treat the literal string NULL as a Java null — useful when null is one of the values you need to test in a multi-argument case
- @CsvFileSource(resources = "/test-cases.csv") for large datasets that do not fit readably inline in the annotation

**@MethodSource for complex objects**
- The factory method returns Stream<Arguments>: Stream.of(Arguments.of(order1, expected1), Arguments.of(order2, expected2))
- This is the only option for testing with domain objects or any test data that requires construction logic — @ValueSource and @CsvSource only support primitive types and strings
- External factory: @MethodSource("com.example.TestData#orderCases") keeps test files clean by moving test data to a shared utility class

Display names prevent mystery failures — @ParameterizedTest(name = "order {0} status {1}") shows argument values in the failure message; without this you get "test[3]" and must guess which case failed.

sections.title: The try-catch Anti-Pattern — Why Your Exception Test Might Not Be Testing Anything
Testing Exception Messages, Causes, and Custom Fields
Parameterized Exception Testing — Multiple Invalid Inputs, One Test Method
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The most common exception testing mistake is wrapping the call in a try-catch. If no exception is thrown, the fail() call inside the catch block is never reached and the test passes silently — exactly when it should fail. JUnit 5's assertThrows eliminates this mistake structurally.

**assertThrows — the correct approach**
- ValidationException thrown = assertThrows(ValidationException.class, () -> service.process(null)) — if no exception is thrown, assertThrows fails the test immediately; if a different exception type is thrown, it also fails with the actual type reported
- The return value is the thrown exception — assert on the message, cause, or any custom field: assertThat(thrown.getMessage()).contains("required")
- assertThrows is type-safe: the lambda must throw the exact type you specified, not a parent type — assertThrows(Exception.class, ...) passes for any exception and is too broad to be useful

**assertDoesNotThrow — negative testing**
- assertDoesNotThrow(() -> service.process(validInput)) explicitly tests the happy path does not throw — clearer than a test with no exception assertion, which is ambiguous about whether the absence of an exception is intentional
- Useful in parameterized tests where some inputs should throw and others should not — make the intent explicit in both directions

**Exception cause chains with AssertJ**
- When your code wraps exceptions: assertThatThrownBy(() -> repo.save(entity)).isInstanceOf(DataAccessException.class).hasCauseInstanceOf(ConstraintViolationException.class) navigates the cause chain
- JUnit 5 alone does not easily test cause chains — assertThrows(DataAccessException.class, ...) does not assert the wrapped cause; AssertJ handles this in one fluent expression

**Common mistakes**
- try { call(); fail(); } catch (Exception e) { ... } passes silently when no exception is thrown because fail() inside catch is unreachable; always use assertThrows
- Catching Exception.class instead of the specific type — does not catch you if a different exception is thrown by mistake

- **Do not catch Exception.class** — too broad; passes for any exception type including unexpected ones; always specify the exact expected exception class
- **assertDoesNotThrow makes intent explicit** — use in parameterized tests where some inputs throw and others do not; clearer than a test with no exception assertion

sections.title: A Good Test Is a Specification — A Bad Test Is a Maintenance Burden
sections.content:
Unit tests serve two purposes: **catching regressions** and **documenting behavior.** A test named `testMethod1` that asserts on random implementation details catches regressions poorly (breaks on any refactor) and documents nothing. A test named `shouldRejectOrderWhenInventoryInsufficient` that tests behavior through the public API catches real bugs and serves as executable documentation.

Three principles separate maintainable tests from fragile ones:

**Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA):** Every test has three distinct sections. Arrange sets up the test data and mocks. Act calls the method under test. Assert verifies the result. Clear separation makes tests readable at a glance. When a test mixes setup, execution, and verification in interleaved calls, no one can tell what's being tested.

**Test isolation:** Each test must be independent — runnable alone, in any order, without shared state. Tests that depend on execution order (test A creates data that test B reads) are the most common source of flaky tests. Use `@BeforeEach` for setup, not class-level mutable fields that survive between tests.

**Behavior over implementation:** Test what the code does, not how it does it. If you test that a service calls `repository.save()` followed by `cache.put()` in exactly that order, every refactoring breaks the test. If you test that after creating a user, the user is retrievable and a notification was sent — that's behavior.

sections.title: Naming, Structure, and the One-Assertion Guideline
Test Isolation — The Difference Between Tests That Always Pass and Tests That Sometimes Fail
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Unit tests serve two purposes simultaneously — catching regressions and documenting behavior. A test named testMethod1 that asserts on internal implementation details serves neither. A test named shouldRejectOrderWhenInventoryInsufficient that tests observable behavior under a meaningful scenario serves both.

**Test naming — behavior not implementation**
- Use shouldDoXWhenY or givenX_whenY_thenZ naming — the test name is the documentation; a reader should understand what behavior is proven without reading the assertion code
- Never name tests after implementation details — testPrivateHelper or testSetStatus — these names break on any refactoring and document nothing about the requirement
- The test name is the first thing a failing CI notification shows — a descriptive name immediately tells the reviewer what regressed

**Arrange-Act-Assert structure**
- Arrange: set up the test data and mock behavior — keep this section minimal; if setup is long it is a signal the class under test has too many dependencies or responsibilities
- Act: a single method call — exactly one action per test; multiple actions in one test make it unclear which action caused a failure when the test reports red
- Assert: verify the outcome using AssertJ for clear failure messages; assert on behavior — what the caller observes — not on implementation — which private method was called

**Test isolation**
- Each test must be independent — no shared mutable state between test methods, no reliance on execution order; JUnit 5 creates a new test instance for each method by default, which helps enforce this
- @BeforeEach for shared setup that applies to every test; avoid @BeforeAll for mutable state — static mutable state shared across all tests is a fragile coupling that causes order-dependent failures
- Avoid @TestMethodOrder unless documenting an intentional interaction scenario

**Test behavior, not implementation**
- A test that verifies verify(repo).save(any()) is testing implementation — if you refactor to saveAndFlush(), the test breaks even though behavior is unchanged
- A test that verifies order.status() == CONFIRMED is testing behavior — it passes regardless of which internal repository method you called

sections.content:
- **Name tests as specifications** — shouldRejectOrderWhenInventoryInsufficient documents behavior; testMethod1 documents nothing; the name is the first CI failure signal
- **Arrange-Act-Assert** — one clear arrange section, one method call as the act, one focused assertion; multiple actions in one test make failure diagnosis ambiguous
- **Test independence** — each test starts clean; no shared mutable state; no execution-order dependency; JUnit 5's new-instance-per-method default enforces this automatically
- **Test behavior not implementation** — assertThat(order.status()).isEqualTo(CONFIRMED) survives refactoring; verify(repo).save(any()) breaks when internal calls change even if behavior is identical
- **Long arrange section = design signal** — if test setup requires five mock configurations, the class under test has too many dependencies; the test is revealing a design problem

beats.text: Unit tests serve two purposes: catching regressions and documenting behavior. A test named testMethod1 that asserts on random implementation details catches regressions poorly (breaks on any refactor) and documents nothing. A test named shouldRejectOrderWhenInventoryInsufficient that tests behavior through the public API catches real bugs and serves as executable documentation. Three principles separate maintainable tests from fragile ones: Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA): Every test has three distinct sections. Arrange sets up the test data and mocks. Act calls the method under test. Assert verifies the result. Clear separation makes tests readable at a glance. When a test mixes setup, execution, and verification in interleaved calls, no one can tell what's being tested. Test isolation: Each test must be independent — runnable alone, in.
